course_title: The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine

series.title: Papers you can see: Brin & Page 1998
series.audience: curious beginners with no maths beyond percentages

shorts.title: PageRank: the random surfer
shorts.hook: Brin and Page ranked the whole web with one imaginary person who clicks links forever. Where does that person spend their time?
shorts.claim: A page's PageRank is the long-run share of time a random surfer spends on it, so one link from a busy page can beat many links from quiet ones.

worked_example.setup: Four pages A, B, C, D with links A->B, A->C, B->C, C->A, D->C. Damping d = 0.85: each step the surfer follows a random link on the current page with probability 0.85, or jumps to any of the 4 pages with probability 0.15 (so every page gets 0.15/4 = 3.75% of each step for free). Start with 25% on every page.
steps: Step 1, C: it receives half of A's 25%, all of B's 25% and all of D's 25%, so 0.85 x 62.5% + 3.75% = 56.875%, about 57%.
Repeating the same update, the shares swing (A after steps 1 to 8: 25, 52, 29, 39, 39, 35, 38, 37 percent) and settle by about step 12 to A 37.3%, B 19.6%, C 39.4%, D 3.75%.

Check: exact solution of the linear equations gives A = 659/1769, B = 27713/141520, C = 2789/7076, D = 3/80; a simulated surfer taking 1,000,000 random steps visits A 37.2%, B 19.6%, C 39.4%, D 3.75% of the time.
worked_example.result: PageRank (rounded) A 37%, B 20%, C 39%, D 4%. A has a single incoming link yet ranks almost level with C, which has three, because A's one link comes from C, the busiest page, and C sends A everything. D has no incoming links and keeps only the 3.75% from random jumps.

shorts.visual: One 4-node link graph (A, B, C, D with five arrows) fills the upper stage; under it a bar chart with one bar per page and a percent label. A glowing surfer dot hops along arrows and occasionally teleports while visit counters grow; then the bars switch to the probability-flow view: each page's share splits along its out-arrows as small blobs, 15% rains down evenly, the bars update step by step and visibly settle at 37, 20, 39, 4. A highlight compares A's single incoming arrow from C with C's three incoming arrows.
shorts.misconception: PageRank is not a count of incoming links: A has one incoming link and C has three, yet they end up almost tied, because a link passes on the linking page's own rank divided by its number of out-links.

practice.question: If D also got a link from C (so C links to A and D), would A's rank go up or down, and why?
practice.answer: Down: C would split its share between A and D, so A receives only half of C's rank instead of all of it.

Related-work survey of earlier engines and IR; no single checkable mechanism.
System architecture (crawler, indexer, barrels, inverted index); a good future short but out of scope for the single requested PageRank short.
Measurements and storage tables from 1998 hardware; numbers to report, not an idea to animate.
Conclusions and future-work list; summary material only.
Appendix argument about advertising incentives; an opinion essay, no mechanism.
